The Leopard-spotted goby, Thorogobius ephippiatus, is a small benthic fish inhabiting rocky reefs and subtidal zones of the northeastern Atlantic. Field surveys and laboratory measurements have provided a detailed understanding of its life-history parameters. Neonates emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs that measure approximately 2 millimeters in length and 0.9 millimeters in width, yielding a calculated wet weight at birth of just 0.00085 grams [Wwb = 0.00085 grams], a value that underscores the minute size of the prolarvae at the moment of eclosion. This initial mass is remarkably low, reflecting the modest energetic reserves packaged within each yolk-laden egg prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a relatively modest body size, with puberty being attained at a total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 1.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.9 grams] as estimated from length-weight regressions. Individuals continue somatic growth after reaching reproductive maturity, eventually achieving a maximum or ultimate total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], which translates into a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 20.6 grams [Wwi = 20.6 grams] based on the same allometric scaling relationship. This substantial increase in mass from puberty to adulthood indicates a prolonged period of post-maturational growth, a pattern common among gobies.

Reproductive output in Thorogobius ephippiatus has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions reflecting the ambient thermal regime of its native habitat. At a stable water temperature of 11.4 °C [T = 11.4 °C], females are capable of an impressive annual reproductive effort. Detailed spawning observations indicate that each female produces approximately 33 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 33 eggs per clutch], and that multiple clutches are deposited throughout the breeding season, with a frequency of about one clutch per day [F_R_i = about one clutch per day]. This daily spawning schedule, sustained over months, yields a remarkably high reproductive output for a fish of this body size.

Lifespan data for the Leopard-spotted goby, also recorded under the same thermal conditions, indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] at 11.4 °C [T = 11.4 °C]. This extended lifespan, which is substantial for a small cryptobenthic fish, is likely linked to the species' occupation of stable, low-predation rocky crevice habitats and its relatively slow pace of life. The combination of a long reproductive window with sustained high fecundity per unit time suggests that lifetime reproductive output is considerable, with individuals potentially spawning over many consecutive seasons before succumbing to senescence.

Comparative life-history data place Thorogobius ephippiatus among the longer-lived and more fecund members of the Gobiidae. The ultimate total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] is moderate for the genus, yet the capacity for daily spawning over a multi-year reproductive lifespan is noteworthy. The wet weight at birth of 0.00085 grams [Wwb = 0.00085 grams] is consistent with the tiny egg size typical of gobies that produce numerous, small pelagic or adhesive propagules. These traits, when viewed together, paint a picture of a species that relies on high fecundity and a protracted breeding period to offset the presumed high mortality rates of its diminutive pelagic larvae.
